{{Short description|Concept in statistical physics}}
In [[statistical physics]], the '''classical Heisenberg model''', developed by [[Werner Heisenberg]], is the <math>n = 3</math> case of the [[n-vector model|''n''-vector model]], one of the models used  to model [[ferromagnetism]] and other phenomena.

==Definition==
The classical Heisenberg model can be formulated as follows: take a d-dimensional [[lattice (group)|lattice]], and place a set of spins of unit length,

:<math>\vec{s}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3, |\vec{s}_i|=1\quad (1)</math>,

on each lattice node.

The model is defined through the following [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]]:
: <math>\mathcal{H} = -\sum_{i,j} \mathcal{J}_{ij} \vec{s}_i \cdot \vec{s}_j\quad (2)</math>
where
: <math> \mathcal{J}_{ij} = \begin{cases} J & \mbox{if }i, j\mbox{ are neighbors} \\ 0 & \mbox{else.}\end{cases}</math>

is a coupling between spins.

The classical Heisenberg model is the [[semiclassical physics|semiclassical limit]] of the isotropic spin-''s'' [[quantum Heisenberg model]] in the limit as ''s'' becomes large.

==Properties==
* The general mathematical formalism used to describe and solve the Heisenberg model and certain generalizations is developed in the article on the [[Potts model]].
* In the [[continuum limit]] the Heisenberg model (2) gives the following equation of motion
:: <math>\vec{S}_{t}=\vec{S}\wedge \vec{S}_{xx}. </math>
:This equation is called the [[continuous classical Heisenberg ferromagnet equation]] or, more shortly, the Heisenberg model and is [[Integrable system|integrable]] in the sense of soliton theory. It admits several integrable and nonintegrable generalizations like the [[Landau–Lifshitz model|Landau-Lifshitz equation]], the [[Ishimori equation]], and so on.

===One dimension===
*In the case of a long-range interaction, <math> J_{x,y}\sim |x-y|^{-\alpha} </math>, the thermodynamic limit is well defined if  <math> \alpha >1 </math>; the magnetization remains zero if <math> \alpha \ge 2 </math>; but the magnetization is positive, at a low enough temperature, if  <math> 1< \alpha < 2 </math> (infrared bounds).
*As in any 'nearest-neighbor' [[n-vector model]] with free boundary conditions, if the external field is zero, there exists a simple exact solution.

===Two dimensions===
* In the case of a long-range interaction, <math> J_{x,y}\sim |x-y|^{-\alpha} </math>, the thermodynamic limit is well defined if <math> \alpha >2 </math>; the magnetization remains zero if <math> \alpha \ge 4 </math>; but the magnetization is positive at a low enough temperature if  <math> 2< \alpha <  4 </math> (infrared bounds).
* Polyakov has conjectured that, as opposed to the [[classical XY model]], there is no [[dipole phase]] for any <math>T>0</math>; namely, at non-zero temperatures the correlations cluster exponentially fast.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Polyakov|first=A.M.|journal=Phys. Lett.|year=1975|volume=B 59|issue=1|pages=79–81|title=Interaction of goldstone particles in two dimensions. Applications to ferromagnets and massive Yang-Mills fields|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(75)90161-6|bibcode = 1975PhLB...59...79P }}</ref>

===Three and higher dimensions===
Independently of the range of the interaction, at a low enough temperature the magnetization is positive.

Conjecturally, in each of the low temperature  extremal states the truncated correlations decay algebraically.
